memories.content: Use a flow diagram rather than a sequence table when alternate procedural branches lead to different outcomes.
Draw alternate branches and their resulting outcomes in the same flow diagram so readers can compare them at once.
The visual fidelity of a prototype may differ from its functional fidelity.
A flow diagram can make alternate branches and their different outcomes visible in one view.
HCI reviewers often skim prototype screens and interaction flow diagrams before reading the main text.
Readers can understand the overall branching shape of a procedure more quickly from a flow diagram than from rows read one at a time.
Redrawing a branching flow diagram after a procedural change usually takes longer than updating one row in a table.
Reviewers often inspect the proposal’s main visual before reading the procedural explanation in full.
Keep the main text to the total and major categories, and place quantities, unit rates, and assumptions in one compact budget table or appendix.
Give each cost category, quantity, unit rate, and subtotal a stable row in the separate budget table.
Put the estimate basis in a dedicated table column so one assumption can be checked or revised without rewriting the narrative.
Readers can verify arithmetic and compare categories faster in a consistent table than in amounts distributed across prose.
Revise one table row and its subtotal when an estimate changes instead of repeating the new amount across several prose paragraphs.
Keep detailed arithmetic out of the main argument when readers can reach the complete table from a clear reference.
The user tends to interrupt the argument with long cost enumerations when no separate budget table is available.

analysis.overview: The frames offer complementary, scope-dependent guidance on choosing and maintaining visual structures. Branching procedures favor flow diagrams, while budgets favor compact tables. One-sided context covers prototype fidelity, reviewer reading behavior, budget-table structure, and a tendency toward disruptive cost detail.

relations.reason: The recommendations address the same presentation decision under explicit content conditions: branches and outcomes benefit from a unified flow view, while quantities, arithmetic, and major budget categories benefit from a reachable table rather than distributed prose.
relations.summary: Use a flow diagram for branching procedures and a compact table for detailed budgets, keeping each information type in a form that supports rapid comparison and preserves a concise main narrative.

relations.reason: Both claims concern revising structured information, but their explicit representational scopes explain the different update methods and must be preserved.
relations.summary: Maintenance effort depends on the representation: procedural changes may require redrawing a branching diagram, whereas estimate changes can be confined to one budget row and subtotal.

relations.reason: This independently useful distinction appears only in the reference frame and is not addressed by the budget-presentation guidance.
relations.summary: A prototype’s visual fidelity can differ from its functional fidelity.

relations.reason: The reference memories restate one one-sided claim about reviewer reading order; the compared frame supplies no corresponding reviewer-behavior claim.
relations.summary: Reviewers often inspect prototype screens, interaction flows, or the proposal’s main visual before reading the full explanation.

relations.reason: These compared-frame memories split one underlying table-design claim that has no counterpart in the reference frame’s flow-diagram guidance.
relations.summary: Organize budget details with stable category rows and a dedicated estimate-basis column so individual values or assumptions can be checked and revised independently.

relations.reason: This is a one-sided observation about user behavior, distinct from the frames’ general presentation and maintenance policies.
relations.summary: Without a separate budget table, the user tends to interrupt the argument with long cost enumerations.

reports.compared_only: Budget tables benefit from stable category rows and a dedicated assumption column; without a separate table, the user tends to interrupt arguments with lengthy cost enumerations.
reports.differences: Representation depends on content: flow diagrams expose procedural branches and outcomes, whereas compact tables support budget verification and concise argument. Their maintenance guidance likewise contrasts diagram redrawing with isolated row updates.
reports.reference_only: Prototype visual and functional fidelity may diverge, and reviewers often inspect central visuals before reading explanations fully.
